TargetRLF1: Sexually transmitted infections (STIs), also known as sexually transmitted diseases (STDs), are infections that are typically spread through sexual contact, including vaginal, anal, or oral sex. These infections can be caused by bacteria, viruses, or parasites, and they can have serious health consequences if left untreated. Common STIs include chlamydia, gonorrhoea, syphilis, genital herpes, human papillomavirus (HPV), and HIV/AIDS ayo Here are some ways to prevent the transmission of STIs:  Abstinence: The most effective way to prevent STIs is to abstain from sexual activity (vaginal, anal, or oral) with a partner who has an STI or whose STI status is unknown.  Use Condoms: Consistently and correctly using condoms during sexual activity can significantly reduce the risk of STI transmission. Use latex or polyurethane condoms for vaginal or anal sex, and use condoms or dental dams for oral sex.  Limit Sexual Partners: Having fewer sexual partners reduces your risk of exposure to STIs. Mutual monogamy with a partner who has tested negative for STIs can also lower your risk.  Communication: Talk openly and honestly with your sexual partners about STIs, testing, and safer sex practices. Encourage each other to get tested regularly for STIs.  Get Tested: Get tested for STIs regularly, especially if you are sexually active with multiple partners or have had unprotected sex. Many STIs do not cause symptoms, so testing is the only way to know your STI status.  Vaccination: Vaccines are available to prevent certain STIs, such as HPV and hepatitis B. Talk to your healthcare provider about whether vaccination is appropriate for you.  Avoid Sharing Needles: If you use injectable drugs, never share needles or other drug paraphernalia. Sharing needles can transmit STIs such as HIV and hepatitis B and C.  Practice Safer Sex: Avoid high-risk sexual behaviors, such as unprotected sex with multiple partners or engaging in sex while under the influence of drugs or alcohol. Use your best judgment and prioritize your health and safety.  Routine Health Care: Attend regular check-ups with your healthcare provider for sexual health screenings and preventive care. Seek medical attention promptly if you experience symptoms of an STI or have been exposed to an STI.  By practicing safer sex, getting tested regularly, and communicating openly with your sexual partners, you can reduce your risk of contracting STIs and protect your sexual health. If you have questions or concerns about STI prevention, don't hesitate to speak with a healthcare provider or sexual health professional for guidance and support.

Use Condoms: Consistently and correctly using condoms during sexual activity can significantly reduce the risk of STI transmission. Use latex or polyurethane condoms for vaginal or anal sex, and use condoms or dental dams for oral sex.  Limit Sexual Partners: Having fewer sexual partners reduces your risk of exposure to STIs. Mutual monogamy with a partner who has tested negative for STIs can also lower your risk.  Communication: Talk openly and honestly with your sexual partners about STIs, testing, and safer sex practices. Encourage each other to get tested regularly for STIs. Talk to your healthcare provider about whether vaccination is appropriate for you.  Avoid Sharing Needles: If you use injectable drugs, never share needles or other drug paraphernalia. Sharing needles can transmit STIs such as HIV and hepatitis B and C.  Practice Safer Sex: Avoid high-risk sexual behaviors, such as unprotected sex with multiple partners or engaging in sex while under the influence of drugs or alcohol. Seek medical attention promptly if you experience symptoms of an STI or have been exposed to an STI. Common STIs include chlamydia, gonorrhoea, syphilis, genital herpes, human papillomavirus (HPV), and HIV/AIDS ayo Here are some ways to prevent the transmission of STIs:  Abstinence: The most effective way to prevent STIs is to abstain from sexual activity (vaginal, anal, or oral) with a partner who has an STI or whose STI status is unknown.  Use Condoms: Consistently and correctly using condoms during sexual activity can significantly reduce the risk of STI transmission. Use latex or polyurethane condoms for vaginal or anal sex, and use condoms or dental dams for oral sex.  Limit Sexual Partners: Having fewer sexual partners reduces your risk of exposure to STIs. Mutual monogamy with a partner who has tested negative for STIs can also lower your risk.  Communication: Talk openly and honestly with your sexual partners about STIs, testing, and safer sex practices. Encourage each other to get tested regularly for STIs.  Get Tested: Get tested for STIs regularly, especially if you are sexually active with multiple partners or have had unprotected sex. Many STIs do not cause symptoms, so testing is the only way to know your STI status.  Vaccination: Vaccines are available to prevent certain STIs, such as HPV and hepatitis B. Talk to your healthcare provider about whether vaccination is appropriate for you.  Avoid Sharing Needles: If you use injectable drugs, never share needles or other drug paraphernalia. Sharing needles can transmit STIs such as HIV and hepatitis B and C.  Practice Safer Sex: Avoid high-risk sexual behaviors, such as unprotected sex with multiple partners or engaging in sex while under the influence of drugs or alcohol. Use your best judgment and prioritize your health and safety.  Routine Health Care: Attend regular check-ups with your healthcare provider for sexual health screenings and preventive care. Seek medical attention promptly if you experience symptoms of an STI or have been exposed to an STI.  By practicing safer sex, getting tested regularly, and communicating openly with your sexual partners, you can reduce your risk of contracting STIs and protect your sexual health. If you have questions or concerns about STI prevention, don't hesitate to speak with a healthcare provider or sexual health professional for guidance and support.

Additionally, preventive measures, such as safe sex practices and access to pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), can reduce the risk of HIV transmission.

TargetRLF1: Chlamydia also known as Chlamydial Genitourinary Infection often has no symptoms, but it can cause serious health problems, even without symptoms. If symptoms occur, they may not appear until several weeks after having sex with a partner who has chlamydia. Even when chlamydia has no symptoms, it can damage a woman's reproductive system. Women with symptoms of Genital infection may notice: An abnormal vaginal discharge, A burning sensation when peeing. Men with symptoms of Genital infection may notice: A discharge from their penis, A burning sensation when peeing, Pain and swelling in one or both testicles (although this is less common). Symptoms from rectal infections. Men and women can also get chlamydia in their rectum. This happens either by having receptive anal sex, or by spread from another infected site (such as the vagina). While these infections often cause no symptoms, they can cause: Rectal pain, Discharge, Bleeding. If a patient has Lymphogranuloma Venereum (LGV), initial symptoms may include genital ulcers, followed by painful swelling of lymph nodes in the groin. If untreated, it can lead to severe complications such as rectal strictures.  Throat infections can cause symptoms such as swelling in the back of the throat and mild sore throat, but symptoms are rare.

TargetRLF1: While some people with Genital Herpes or Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV), also known as herpes will never have any symptoms, other people can develop symptoms within a few weeks of being infected. Common oral herpes symptoms include blisters (cold sores) or open sores (ulcers) in or around the mouth or lips. Most people notice a group or cluster of blisters or ulcers (lesions). These lesions burn and can be painful. They can appear on the buttocks, anus or thighs, on the vulva or vagina in women, and on the penis or scrotum in men. Often, before the lesions appear, patients describe a prodrome, characterized by a tingling or burning sensation in the area where the lesions will develop that can be noticed during urination, along with itching or discomfort in the genital area. You can also have the following symptoms, Blisters on the mouth or lips, Fever, headache or pain in the joints, Trouble urinating. In case of Neonatal Herpes, signs that your baby may have herpes are:irritability, blisters anywhere on her body, trouble breathing, grunting, blue appearance (cyanosis), rapid breathing, short periods of no breathing, jaundice, bleeding easily. People can have repeated outbreaks over time (‘recurrences’). These are usually shorter and less severe than the first outbreak. Herpes is a lifelong sexually transmitted infection, that cannot be cured. However, the number of outbreaks/recurrences may reduce over time.

TargetRLF1: A chlamydia also known as Chlamydial Genitourinary infection test detects the bacteria that cause chlamydia, a sexually transmitted infection (STI). This test tells you if you have the chlamydia infection so that you can get treat treatment and avoid complications. Results are usually ready in a day. Less often, providers use a cell culture to test for chlamydia. Or they may use a cell culture to see how chlamydia treatments are working. Because of the possibility of multiple sexually transmitted infections, all patients with any sexually transmitted disease (STD) should be evaluated for chlamydial infection. There are no risks involved with these tests. Rarely the results of the tests may be inconclusive or unclear and you may need to give another sample.

A pregnant person with chlamydia can give the infection to their baby during childbirth and that can cause a type of eye infection in the baby which can damage their sight.

Because of the possibility of multiple sexually transmitted infections, all patients with any sexually transmitted disease (STD) should be evaluated for chlamydial infection. TargetRLF1: Herpes can only be diagnosed at a health centre. You cannot test for it at home or using radiological methods. When a person has active herpes lesions (a.k.a. blisters, sores, ulcers), your healthcare provider may diagnose genital herpes by simply looking at any sores that are present, or a swab can be taken and tests done that can detect the virus directly. The tests used include culture and Nucleic Acid Amplification Testing (NAAT). Both culture and NAAT tests can identify the specific herpes virus type someone is infected with, but NAAT methods are more sensitive. Culture can easily miss infections and give false negative results. Because a culture works by requiring virus that is active, if a lesion is very small, or is already beginning to heal, there may not be enough virus present for an accurate culture. Beyond 48 hours of the symptoms appearing, there is a risk of receiving a false negative test result. The organism that causes the disease was first discovered in 1879 in Albert Neisser, hence the organisma being called Neisseria Gonorrhoea. The word Gonorrhea itself derives from the Greek, meaning "the flow of seed" (gono: seed, rhea: flow).

Because of the possibility of multiple sexually transmitted infections, all patients with any sexually transmitted disease (STD) should be evaluated for chlamydial infection.

TargetRLF1: HIV (Human Immunodeficiency Virus) is a virus that can lead to AIDS (Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome) if left untreated. Once someone becomes infected with HIV, they have the virus for life. There is currently no cure for HIV, and the virus cannot be completely eliminated from the body. However, with proper medical care and treatment, the virus can be controlled, and the progression to AIDS can be prevented. The goal of HIV treatment, known as antiretroviral therapy (ART), is to reduce the viral load (the amount of virus in the blood) to undetectable levels. When the virus is undetectable, it is less likely to be transmitted to others, and the individual with HIV can lead a healthy life. In those days, men were considered victims and women as the source of the disease. The organism that causes the disease was first discovered in 1879 in Albert Neisser, hence the organisma being called Neisseria Gonorrhoea. The word Gonorrhea itself derives from the Greek, meaning "the flow of seed" (gono: seed, rhea: flow).

TargetRLF1: Herpes can only be diagnosed at a health centre. You cannot test for it at home or using radiological methods. When a person has active herpes lesions (a.k.a. blisters, sores, ulcers), your healthcare provider may diagnose genital herpes by simply looking at any sores that are present, or a swab can be taken and tests done that can detect the virus directly. The tests used include culture and Nucleic Acid Amplification Testing (NAAT). Both culture and NAAT tests can identify the specific herpes virus type someone is infected with, but NAAT methods are more sensitive. Culture can easily miss infections and give false negative results. Because a culture works by requiring virus that is active, if a lesion is very small, or is already beginning to heal, there may not be enough virus present for an accurate culture. Beyond 48 hours of the symptoms appearing, there is a risk of receiving a false negative test result. Viral culture is even less accurate during recurrences (positive in only about 30% of recurrent outbreaks). NAAT methods are the preferred method, with PCR as the most-widely used NAAT method. These tests are fast, accurate, and can tell if a person has HSV-1 or HSV-2. There is also less chance of a false negative result with NAATs. If sores are not present, a blood test may be used to look for HSV antibodies. Blood tests can be used when a person has no symptoms but has concerns about having Herpes. Blood tests do not actually detect the virus but look for antibodies.

Akawuka akaleeta obulwadde buno kaasooka kuzuulwa mu mwaka 1879 mu Albert Neisser, noolwekyo akawuka ne katuumibwa Neisseria Gonorrhoea. Ekigambo Enziku kiva mu Luyonaani, ekitegeeza "okukulukuta kw'ensigo."

Hivi ndivyo PrEP inavyofanya kazi: Kinga ya Maambukizi ya virusi vya ukimwi, Matumizi ya Thabiti, Idadi ya Watu Walio Hatarini, Kujilinda, Ufuatiliaji, na Matumizi Yanayofaa. Ni muhimu kutambua kwamba PrEP hailinde dhidi ya magonjwa mengine ya zinaa (STIs) au mimba. Kutumia kondomu na kufanya ngono salama ni muhimu kwa ulinzi wa kina dhidi ya magonjwa ya zinaa na mimba. Watu wanaozingatia PrEP wanapaswa kushauriana na watoa huduma wao wa afya kwa mwongozo wa kama ni chaguo sahihi na kwa ushauri kuhusu matumizi na ufuatiliaji ufaao.
